claims.claim: Choice screens are often presented as modest competition measures.
Choice-screen proposals are commonly premised on displaying several services, allowing users to select one, and relying on that selection to produce market competition.
Platforms can make technical integration, billing support, or safety review conditions of eligibility for a choice screen.
Platforms can determine whether a service qualifies before launch or only after a delay.
Platforms can control the labels used to describe services on choice screens.
Defaults convert the design of a choice screen into corresponding user behavior.
First position, highlighted buttons, and preselected services reduce the effort users need to continue through a choice flow.
Selecting alternatives on choice screens generally requires an additional tap or decision.
Selecting an alternative may trigger an additional warning.
Small interface frictions can accumulate to produce a meaningful behavioral burden.
Defaults can help devices function immediately, especially during setup.
Providers listed on choice screens compete to be selected.
Gatekeepers controlling choice screens also control providers' access to the selection process, including updates and removal.
Gatekeepers can collect information about which options succeed on a choice screen.
Gatekeepers can use option-performance information to revise choice-screen design and thereby obtain a feedback advantage.
The proposed oversight safeguards protect rival companies from harmful gatekeeper treatment.
The proposed oversight safeguards protect buyers' ability to choose an alternative service that can function.
